transcript.text: Section one. You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman and a member of staff at a community sports centre. First you have some time to look at questions one to ten.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Good morning, Fairfield Community Sports Centre, Rosa speaking.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Oh, hello. I'd like to join the centre, if that's possible over the phone.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Of course. I'll take your details. Can I start with your full name?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: It's Daniel Ashcroft. Ashcroft is spelled A-S-H-C-R-O-F-T.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Thank you. And your date of birth?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: The twelfth of March, nineteen ninety-four.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Lovely. What's the best address for us?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Forty-two Wilton Road. That's W-I-L-T-O-N.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: And a contact number?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Oh seven double seven, nine oh four, three one six.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Perfect. Now, we have three types of membership. There's Standard, which is thirty-two pounds a month, Off-Peak at twenty-four, and Family at fifty-five.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I only really get here in the mornings, so the Off-Peak one sounds right.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: That's the sensible choice then. Off-Peak runs until four in the afternoon on weekdays, and all day at weekends.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: That works. What about the pool?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: The pool is included, but do note it closes on Tuesdays for maintenance.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Right, I'll avoid Tuesdays. Do I need to bring anything on my first visit?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Just some photo identification, and we'll take your picture for the card here.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: And is there parking?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: There is, but it's for two hours only unless you buy a permit, which is fifteen pounds a year.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I'll probably walk. One last thing, when does the membership actually start?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: We'll activate it on the first of next month, so you get a full month.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Excellent. Thank you very much.
That is the end of section one. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
Section two. You will hear a talk given to new volunteers at a city botanic garden. First you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: Welcome, everybody, and thank you for giving up your Saturday. I'm Priya, and I coordinate the volunteer programme here at the garden.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: A little history first. The garden was founded in eighteen eighty-six by a local textile manufacturer who wanted somewhere for mill workers to walk on a Sunday.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: It covers eleven hectares, which makes it the second largest green space in the city after the main park.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: We hold around four thousand plant species, and about a fifth of those are grown from seed collected in the wild.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: Now, the practical side. Volunteers work in one of four teams. The propagation team works in the glasshouses and needs no previous experience.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: The borders team does the heavier planting outdoors, so we do ask for a reasonable level of fitness there.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: The third team looks after the herbarium, which is our collection of dried and pressed specimens. That work is indoors and quite detailed.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: And the fourth team runs guided walks for visitors, which means a little training in public speaking, provided free by us.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: Whichever team you join, please sign in at the wooden hut by the east gate, not at the main reception.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: Tools are kept in the shed behind the glasshouses, and the code for the padlock changes every January.

transcript.speaker: Speaker
transcript.text: Finally, lunch. There's a staff room above the shop with a kettle and a fridge, and volunteers get a third off anything in the cafe.
That is the end of section two.
Section three. You will hear two students, Mei and Tom, discussing a project with their tutor. First you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to thirty.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Come in, both of you. How's the river study coming along?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Reasonably well. We've finished the sampling, but we're arguing about how to present it.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Arguing is usually a good sign at this stage. What's the disagreement?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Mei wants to lead with the water chemistry. I think the invertebrate counts tell the story better.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: And why do you think that, Tom?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Because the chemistry only shows what the river was like on the day we sampled. The invertebrates reflect months of conditions.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That's a fair point, and it's the standard argument for biological monitoring. Mei, what's your case?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Only that the chemistry is what our reader will expect. But I take Tom's point, and I'd rather be right than conventional.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Then lead with the invertebrates and use the chemistry to support them. What about the sampling itself, did you manage all six sites?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Five. The sixth was inaccessible after the flooding in February.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That's worth stating plainly in your methods rather than hoping nobody counts. Now, your kick-sampling technique, how long did you sample at each site?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Three minutes, following the standard protocol.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Good. And did you record the substrate type?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: We did, though only as a rough category. Gravel, sand, or silt.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That's enough for this project. What surprised you most?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: The site downstream of the treatment works was healthier than the one upstream. We expected the opposite.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That happens more often than people assume. What explanation are you offering?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: We think it's the shade. The upstream site has no tree cover at all, so it warms up considerably in summer.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Plausible, but you'll need the temperature data to support it. Do you have it?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: We have spot readings, not continuous logging.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Then present it as a hypothesis rather than a conclusion. When can I see a draft?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: We were hoping for the end of next week, if that's not too late.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That's fine. Bring the raw data as well as the write-up.
That is the end of section three.
Section four. You will hear part of a lecture about the history of standardised time. First you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Before the railways, every town in Britain kept its own time, set by the sun. Bristol clocks ran about ten minutes behind London, and nobody found this inconvenient.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: What changed was not technology but scheduling. A timetable is meaningless if the two ends of the line disagree about when noon is.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: The Great Western Railway adopted London time across its network in eighteen forty, and other companies followed within the decade.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: For some years the two systems ran side by side. A number of town clocks were fitted with a second minute hand showing railway time.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Resistance was real, and it was mostly legal rather than sentimental. Court cases turned on which time a contract referred to.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: The most cited example is a case in eighteen fifty-eight in Dorchester, where a hearing was lost because the judge used local time and the defendant arrived on railway time.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Parliament did not settle the matter until eighteen eighty, when Greenwich Mean Time was given legal force throughout Great Britain.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: The international problem was harder, and it was solved by a conference in Washington in eighteen eighty-four, which chose Greenwich as the prime meridian.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: The vote was not unanimous. France abstained, and continued to define its own time by reference to Paris for another quarter of a century.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: What I want you to take from this is that standardisation is rarely a technical achievement. It is almost always a negotiation, and the winner is usually whoever already runs the network.
That is the end of section four. You now have ten minutes to transfer your answers to the answer sheet.

markers.text: Before the railways, every town in Britain kept its own time, set by the sun. Bristol clocks ran about ten minutes behind London, and nobody found this inconvenient.
What changed was not technology but scheduling. A timetable is meaningless if the two ends of the line disagree about when noon is.
The Great Western Railway adopted London time across its network in eighteen forty, and other companies followed within the decade.
For some years the two systems ran side by side. A number of town clocks were fitted with a second minute hand showing railway time.
Resistance was real, and it was mostly legal rather than sentimental. Court cases turned on which time a contract referred to.
The most cited example is a case in eighteen fifty-eight in Dorchester, where a hearing was lost because the judge used local time and the defendant arrived on railway time.
Parliament did not settle the matter until eighteen eighty, when Greenwich Mean Time was given legal force throughout Great Britain.
The international problem was harder, and it was solved by a conference in Washington in eighteen eighty-four, which chose Greenwich as the prime meridian.
The vote was not unanimous. France abstained, and continued to define its own time by reference to Paris for another quarter of a century.
What I want you to take from this is that standardisation is rarely a technical achievement. It is almost always a negotiation, and the winner is usually whoever already runs the network.
